title: I'm a classic old school Conservative, says Kemi Badenoch
description: Kemi Badenoch has declared herself a "classic old school Conservative" as she begins her party's annual conference with a string of policy pledges and
body: Kemi Badenoch has declared herself a "classic old school Conservative" as she begins her party's annual conference with a string of policy pledges and a 100 page statement on her guiding principles., external"I believe in common sense, people working hard and being rewarded for that effort," she told the BBC's Laura Kuenssberg.She added that welfare should be a "safety net, not a lifestyle".The Tory leader is trying to ensure her party stands out in a crowded political field. The Conservatives are trailing Labour and Reform UK in the opinion polls and have yet to recover from their historic defeat at the 2024 general election.Badenoch, whose personal poll ratings are higher than that of her party, has characterised Reform leader Nigel Farage as a "grumpy grandpa" and she told Laura Kuenssberg that Labour leader Andy Burnham is "the cheesy uncle who does all the dad jokes".She described herself as a "no-nonsense mum".Asked if her plan for benefit cuts and a massive increase in prison places was a return to the "nasty party" of the past, she said: "It's the common sense party. That's what we're doing."And, quite frankly, if we were doing so well the old way, then why did we have such a terrible issue in 2024?"In her essay The Right Way - a deliberate echo of an essay written by Margaret Thatcher in 1976, external entitled The Right Approach - Badenoch says the last Conservative government failed because it did not know what it stood for.Despite the party's rhetoric during its 14 years in power, she said: "We did little to reverse the structural changes Labour had made which took the country in the wrong direction. "The result was that the state grew by stealth."The essay says the "next Conservative government will have one central principle: business, not government, creates growth".The Tories would achieve growth through tax cuts, cutting red tape and reducing the size of the civil service back to pre-pandemic levels, the essay says.And it adds: "What is really missing from politics and government today is people prepared to say no. "Political parties now need to recruit those who have the stomach to say no to good causes when the resources simply are not there to do everything."As their conference gets under way in Birmingham the Conservatives have pledged to end a childcare "cliff edge", which currently means parents earning more than £100,000 do not qualify for the entitlement.The party has also promised to deliver 50,000 new prison places by slashing the overseas aid budget to £1bn a year in a bid to end the early release of offenders.Over the 14 years the Conservatives were in power, around 500 net prison places were created, which takes into account 14,142 added in existing and new jails, set against 13,660 lost mainly to dilapidation and closures.Speaking in the main conference hall, Badenoch sought to make the case that the party had moved on from 2024 and outlined her expectation that the next few days in Birmingham would be a chance for members to discuss their ideas.She said: "We're going to be having debates, we're going to have arguments, they are going to be fun."We're going to challenge each other and afterwards we're still going to be a united party."During a question and answer session, Badenoch focused on different topics covered in her essay – including citizenship and how communities need to operate on trust.She said the UK is "not a dormitory, it is not a hotel" before speaking how "British culture means something".To applause in the well-attended hall, Badenoch said: "I don't want lots of little ghettos of separatist communities where they are recreating the place they come from - that will ruin the United Kingdom."Responding, Labour Party chair Bridget Phillipson said the Tory Party "is stuck in the past and remains completely out of touch with what people across Britain want to see"."Last week Andy Burnham set out a plan to bring back hope to Britain. Kemi Badenoch wants to drag our country back to a politics that let so many people down over the past 40 years."

schema.headline: I'm a classic old school Conservative, says Kemi Badenoch

title: British Museum announces changes to ease Bayeux Tapestry queues
description: The British Museum has announced changes to how visitors see the Bayeux Tapestry exhibition after concerns over long queues and overcrowding.The measu
body: The British Museum has announced changes to how visitors see the Bayeux Tapestry exhibition after concerns over long queues and overcrowding.The measures include plans for longer opening hours, as well as an audio guide, additional seating and clearer signage.A museum spokesperson said the public response to the 11th Century embroidery had been "extraordinary", but acknowledged that some visitors had waited longer than they would have wanted.Some people reported waits of up to two hours, while hundreds of ticket holders were reportedly turned away due to backlogs when the museum closed early last week due to a private event.Some ticket holders took to social media to complain about the disruption. One disappointed visitor said the trip had been a "big event" they had looked forward to, while another wrote she had been waiting since she was seven to see the Bayeux Tapestry, and bought tickets only to be turned away after queuing.The museum later apologised to those who had been unable to enter and said they would be issued refunds and priority booking slots for a rearranged time.From Monday, visitors will be offered an audio guide with more information about the embroidery, while additional signage and seating will be provided for those queuing to reach the main exhibition.The museum said it planned to introduce longer opening hours to prevent queues building during the day and allow people with later bookings more time to view the exhibition. Details of the extended hours have not yet been disclosed.Demand for the exhibition has been high since tickets first went on sale in July, with a record 100,000 sold on the first day. Members of the public who were not successful in the first ticket release will have two further chances to view the masterpiece when further tickets go on sale in October and January. Adult tickets cost £33 during peak times and £27 at off-peak hours, compared with its usual €12 (£10) fee to see the tapestry in its home in Bayeux, Normandy. Children under 16 can visit the London exhibition for free. The exhibition opened on 10 September but has experienced a series of problems with queues and congestion, with some visitors spending longer than their allocated 40-minute slot viewing the tapestry.Visitors were later stopped from taking photographs and a recorded message was introduced encouraging people to continue moving through the one-way exhibition.The 70m-long Bayeux Tapestry depicts 58 scenes outlining the extraordinary events surrounding the Norman conquest of England, the Battle of Hastings in 1066 and the end of Anglo-Saxon rule in Britain.Despite its name, the work is an embroidery rather than a tapestry and contains approximately 626 human figures and 200 horses.The Bayeux Tapestry is on loan from the French government, having been transported from its home in Normandy - where it has been exhibited since 1983. It will be on display until July 2027.The loan marks the first time the tapestry has returned to the UK since it was created more than 900 years ago.

schema.headline: British Museum announces changes to ease Bayeux Tapestry queues

title: Ethiopian rebel forces withdraw from Tigray regional capital
description: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, A pro-government soldier standing guard on a street in Ethiopia's Tigray region on SundayByTeklemariam Bekite
body: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, A pro-government soldier standing guard on a street in Ethiopia's Tigray region on SundayByTeklemariam Bekiteditor, BBC Tigrinya, and Jack BurgessRebel forces in Ethiopia's northern Tigray region have said they have temporarily withdrawn from the regional capital, Mekelle, as fighting with the national army moves towards the city.The Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF), which has been running the region, said its decision to relocate was made because of concerns about risks to civilians.Two residents in Mekelle told the BBC that pro-government forces now control the city and TPLF forces have abandoned it. One resident also said mobile phone services appear to have resumed in parts of the city.Fighting has erupted in recent weeks between the TPLF and federal government forces alongside allied fighters in parts of Ethiopia's northern regions of Tigray, Afar and Amhara.The development marks a major shift in the conflict and raises concerns among observers that the fighting could further destabilise the Horn of Africa, potentially drawing in neighbouring countries.The US Department of State called for "restraint" and "dialogue" on all sides ahead of a diplomatic meeting about the conflict in Egypt on Sunday with leaders from some of Ethiopia's neighbours.Tigray residents have been trying to recover from a devastating two-year civil war that ended in 2022 when the African Union (AU) brokered a peace deal, known as the Pretoria Agreement, between the two sides. However, in the last six months there has been a worsening of relations, with both sides accusing each other of violating the agreement.Last month, the TPLF joined six other armed movements, including the Fano militia from Amhara, to form an alliance whose stated objective is to remove Ethiopia's Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed's government from power.The civil war was one of the most deadly conflicts this century - the AU's mediator estimated some 600,000 people died as the fighting drove the region to the precipice of famine.On Friday, neighbours Ethiopia and Eritrea severed diplomatic relations with each other after Addis Ababa accused Asmara of supporting a new rebel alliance - an allegation that it denied.Ethiopia has also accused Egypt of supporting the rebels, leading to the expulsion of an Egyptian diplomat, which Cairo responded to by ordering an Ethiopian embassy official to leave within the same period.The United Nations has warned that the deteriorating security situation in northern Ethiopia is severely disrupting humanitarian work and has called on all sides to guarantee safe and unhindered access to people in need.

schema.headline: Ethiopian rebel forces withdraw from Tigray regional capital

title: Yemen government announces major operation to retake Houthi territory
description: But it is not yet clear whether this represents a new phase in the conflict.The frontline in Yemen remains focused around the key city of Taiz, which
body: But it is not yet clear whether this represents a new phase in the conflict.The frontline in Yemen remains focused around the key city of Taiz, which is still controlled by the internationally recognised government.The Houthis are engaged in a fierce battle with government forces for control of the region, as they seek to secure coastal areas and, by extension, the Bab al-Mandab Strait.On Sunday, the Houthis cut a vital supply route linking Taiz with Aden, the interim capital of the Yemeni government, AFP news agency reports.Citing three Yemeni military sources, AFP also reports that the Houthis now control the area and supply route, effectively encircling Taiz."They've achieved the military objective of isolating Taiz from Aden, even if they haven't fully taken control of it," Farea Al-Muslimi, a research fellow at the Chatham House think tank, told AFP.Away from Yemen, the Houthis are also trying to hurt the Saudis with an attack aimed at the country's economic lifeblood - oil.On Sunday, Yemen's Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said the group had launched a ballistic missile and drone attack on Aramco sites in the capital, Riyadh, and the oil-rich Khurais area in the kingdom's east."Both operations successfully achieved their objectives," the spokesman said in a statement. "The strikes were precise, causing large fires at the targeted sites."It is not the first time the group has said it has hit Saudi oil sites. Saudi Arabia has yet to comment on Sunday's claimed attack, but has previously dismissed some claims as misleading, mocking the Houthis for "chasing imaginary victories".But it has once again shown the price Saudi Arabia - and, as a consequence, the global economy - could pay if it launched a new all-out war against the Houthis.In retaliation, Saudi Arabia has also been striking Houthi targets, according to the Houthi-run Al-Masirah TV channel. It said at least two people had been wounded in strikes on Sunday.On Saturday, Yemen's government also said its forces had hit Houthi targets across the country, including in Sanaa, Saada and the group's positions near Taiz in the south-west.Yemen is one of the poorest countries in the world and remains gripped by a vast humanitarian crisis.A war erupted in 2014, when the Houthis seized the capital, Sanaa, from the Saudi-backed government, before going on to take control of swathes of the country's north.Riyadh intervened in the war the following year, leading an international coalition.After several years of relative calm, the war reignited in July amid the widening conflict in the Middle East.The Houthis have launched a blockade of Saudi energy exports, which have already been squeezed by Iran's closure of the Strait of Hormuz.

schema.headline: Yemen government announces major operation to retake Houthi territory

title: Porridge gurus from opposite sides of globe triumph in world championship
description: The contest rules only allow three ingredients - oats, water and salt. She only started adding salt to her porridge ahead of the competition, but quic
body: The contest rules only allow three ingredients - oats, water and salt. She only started adding salt to her porridge ahead of the competition, but quickly realised it "really brings out the nuances and different aromas". She believes her secret weapon may have been the water which she brought with her from her home city. "It's very soft, and I think the mineral content may have something to do with it. I'm not sure - but it worked last time and this time as well, so maybe it's the water". In the Speciality Porridge category, Rob, from Sydney, came up with his recipe just a few weeks before competing in the Australian national porridge championships - the Pearly  Spurtle   - after realising how seriously everyone was taking it.Tapping into his family heritage - his father is Scottish and his mother is Sicilian - he decided to make a  porridge cannoli."I then had to engineer it," the 36-year-old  told BBC Scotland News.  The cream uses the traditional mix of ricotta, mascarpone and sugar but he blended in porridge,  sieved it and added some ground toasted oats. It provides the filling for shells, made like brandy snaps but using Sicilian Marsala wine instead.

schema.headline: Porridge gurus from opposite sides of globe triumph in world championship

title: I paid £30,000 for an 'influencer' degree. Here's why
description: As university courses go it may raise a few eyebrows, but Destiny McGowan has no doubt that hers was very useful.In July the 21-year-old graduated fro
body: As university courses go it may raise a few eyebrows, but Destiny McGowan has no doubt that hers was very useful.In July the 21-year-old graduated from Nottingham Trent University with a degree in content creation.As well as teaching how to best make videos and posts for Instagram, TikTok and YouTube, the course also focused on how to build audiences, engage with brands and monetise your content."I always wanted to be an entrepreneur, so for me the course was about the transferable skills that I believed I would gain," says Destiny, pointing to both the social media and business aspects she was taught.It's early on in her career, and Destiny won't disclose precisely what she is earning, but says she's already making money.In addition to posting about fashion on her own accounts, she makes videos for others, and has also been hired as a TikTok live selling host, presenting products for sale on camera.She says the course gave her access to equipment, technology and industry contacts."The incredible people I've met through panels that the university hosted would take someone five to 10 years to get to that place," she explains.Nottingham Trent says its content creation degree, which it launched in 2022, provides "hands-on experience". Several universities in the UK now offer such courses. The University of Brighton says it teaches students how to create "content that cuts through the noise".Meanwhile in the US, Arizona State University say its similar qualification allows students to "turn your creativity into content that connects with audiences". Yet you'd be paying a lot of money for this. The three-year degrees at Nottingham Trent and Brighton both currently cost £9,790 per year for UK students, while the standard annual fee at Arizona State is $14,724 (£11,000) for a resident of that state.So are such degrees worth it? Knightenator, a UK-based content creator, isn't sure. "I don't think I would have taken the course," she says.The 31-year-old, who doesn't reveal her real name, has been posting videos about gaming and travel on social media since 2015. She now has 65,000 followers on Twitch, and more than 100,000 on TikTok.Content creation is her full-time job, with brand deals making up most of her income, she says."Honestly, from my experience, I don't think companies would care too much if you had a content creator degree," she says.She adds that the internet is saturated with free advice on how to get started. "If you have the drive to want to become a content creator, the tips are out there, and you don't need to commit to a three-year degree."Her advice is to watch other people's content and find your own niche. "I honestly think that you don't need much in this day and age at this moment to be able to do it."But fellow content creator Aiesha Beasley from Phoenix, Arizona disagrees.The 36-year-old, who posts about food, fashion and lifestyle, says she would have enrolled on one of these courses if they had been available when she first started blogging on Tumblr in the early 2010s.She believes a degree would have given her a "clearer pathway", particularly when it comes to how to earn a living."You really do have to have a business mindset on: how can I transition this from a hobby into something that makes me money?" says Aiesha.She adds that such courses are "ahead of the curve" in recognising that content creation is increasingly an important part of marketing."Now you have to have a digital presence," she explains, "whether you are a business owner or an entrepreneur or building a personal brand."The degrees by the likes of Nottingham Trent and Arizona State come as the content creator economy booms on both sides of the Atlantic. YouTube content creators alone contribute £2.2bn to the UK economy, according to one report last year.Meanwhile, one in three people aged between 18 and 30 in the US wish to become an influencer, a 2024 survey suggests. , externalHowever, Jacky Gurr, course leader and senior lecturer for content creation at Nottingham Trent University, points out that the majority of people on the course are not actually aspiring to become influencers.For Gurr, content creation is a professional skill that organisations increasingly need, whether someone runs their own business, works in-house, joins an agency or works freelance across multiple clients."Those skills absolutely can be taught. Students learn how to plan and produce video content, develop campaigns, understand audiences, analyse performance data and adapt strategies based on that data."She adds that the business side of content creation "is an important part of the degree", where they discuss monetisation and the commercial side of the industry.But for anyone who thinks a university degree will lead to overnight success as an influencer, Jacky Gurr has these words of caution: "So much of being a successful influencer is about luck, and we can't teach luck or personality."

schema.headline: I paid £30,000 for an 'influencer' degree. Here's why

title: Courts backlog will fall despite scrapping plans to curb jury trials, Alex Norris insists
description: The courts backlog will still fall despite plans to curb jury trials being scrapped, the justice secretary has told the BBC.Alex Norris said introduci
body: The courts backlog will still fall despite plans to curb jury trials being scrapped, the justice secretary has told the BBC.Alex Norris said introducing legislation for judge-only trials "was always going to be the most complicated to implement" and would have slowed down reforms.Prime Minister Andy Burnham's decision abandons proposals introduced by Sir Keir Starmer's government to allow judges in England and Wales to make the sole decision on cases that would lead to a sentence of less than three years.The Ministry of Justice (MoJ) said only complex fraud and financial offences would be judge-only - and it proposes thousands of medium-level crimes should stay with volunteer magistrates, who sit without a jury.Norris told the BBC's Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg the backlog would start falling "in this Parliament", but would not say by how much. He said it would fall significantly over the next decade "as a result of the changes we're making". The Conservatives said it was a "major victory" for those who fought to defend trial by jury, while criminal lawyers welcomed the decision but voiced concern about the implications of abolishing a defendant's right to ask for a jury trial.The Criminal Bar Association (CBA) warned this would keep more middle-ranking cases before magistrates and shift 25,000 cases a year onto magistrates' courts.Former justice secretary David Lammy first announced the plans to curb jury trials in December following a recommendation in a major review of the court system in England and Wales.The series of radical reforms, including scaling back jury trials, were presented as the best way of turning around record backlogs which, in turn, were exacerbating the prison population crisis. The backlog - which has led to record delays for defendants and victims - currently stands at nearly 81,000 cases, having rocketed largely thanks to cuts before the pandemic and court closures during national lockdowns. Official projections have estimated it could reach 100,000 before the next general election and, in a worst-case scenario, climb to double that number by 2035. There are, however, indications the backlog is now stabilising after the government committed unlimited funding to pay for more judges to sit in courts that were otherwise being unused. Under the original plans, Lammy had wanted to reserve jury trials for the most serious "indictable" offences - meaning cases that are always sent to Crown Court, including murder and rape. Less serious offences, where the sentence would be no more than three years, would be decided without a jury in the Crown Court by a judge alone. Even less serious offences than that would stay in magistrates' courts, abolishing the right of defendants to ask for a trial by jury when they feel that is their best chance of being cleared.The proposals triggered an outcry across many parts of the criminal justice world, with many opponents saying eroding the 800-year-old right to trial by jury would not solve the backlogs.  Andrew Thomas KC - chairman of the Criminal Bar Association, which represents barristers who work in crown and magistrates courts - said the profession was "delighted". "Justice needs juries," he said. "Nothing inspires more public trust than 12 ordinary citizens from all walks of life deciding the facts of a case together."We are also pleased that the government is going ahead with important changes in the bill to protect victims and witnesses at trial. These include new powers to prevent unfair questioning about a complainant's behaviour and to support witnesses to give their best evidence."But Thomas warned plans to keep more middle-ranking cases before magistrates could backfire - not least because of a shortage of magistrates. "The proposal to strip defendants of their right to elect a crown court trial, combined with doubling magistrates' sentencing powers to two years, would shift 25,000 cases a year - including 5,500 jury trials - out of the crown court," he said."These are not minor offences. It includes serious and sensitive cases including assaults, sexual assaults, child abuse and grievous bodily harm. Our volunteer magistrates do an excellent job but they are completely unequipped to try complex, multi-day trials."It would be a car crash if they tried to do it, especially at this time."Claire Waxman, victims' commissioner for England and Wales, said victims were "being asked to place their faith in a plan that ministers themselves argued would not be [enough]".Barrister Karl Turner, a Labour MP who was suspended from the parliamentary party after he criticised the government's plans to reform jury trials, thanked Burnham "for his support during my campaign".Shadow justice secretary Nick Timothy said: "This is a major victory for everyone who fought to defend trial by jury, and Conservatives led that fight from day one. Labour have been forced to abandon its central attack on jury trials in the Crown Court."Liberal Democrat justice spokeswoman Jess Brown-Fully added the proposal "should never have been introduced in the first place", while Green MP Sian Berry said it was "a victory for justice and fairness".

schema.headline: Courts backlog will fall despite scrapping plans to curb jury trials, Alex Norris insists

title: Sussex horse lover's final wish fulfilled with hospice pony visit
description: Image source, FamilyImage caption, Denise Lee was able to pet the ponies and they laid their heads on her bedBySarah GorrellBBC Radio Sussex and Tanya
body: Image source, FamilyImage caption, Denise Lee was able to pet the ponies and they laid their heads on her bedBySarah GorrellBBC Radio Sussex and Tanya GuptaSouth EastA lifelong horse lover was able to spend time with two ponies in the final days of her life after a community appeal helped arrange a surprise hospice visit.Denise Lee, from Ashington, West Sussex, had loved horses since childhood and volunteered with the Riding for the Disabled Association but her cancer diagnosis meant she could no longer ride.While receiving care at St Barnabas House in Worthing last month, she told the hospice's staff she would love to touch a horse and experience the "horsey smell" again.A healthcare assistant suggested trying to make the wish happen and Joanne, Denise's daughter, appealed for help through local Facebook community groups."She was a horse lover from I think the age of like five or six," Joanne said."She loved all animals, but horses were really special to her. So she rode throughout her whole life."Image source, FamilyImage caption, The grandmother stroked the horses while her family looked onThe post was spotted by Kerry Saunders, from Ashington, who offered to bring two Shetland ponies to the hospice.Staff helped move Denise's bed into a courtyard so she could meet the animals and stroke them, with family members, including her granddaughters, Sassi, aged eight, and Phoebe, aged seven, also there."The horses walked round the corner and there wasn't a dry eye in the place," Joanne said."Everyone was crying. The staff were there. Her grandchildren were there. We were all there. And it was the most special memory."Image source, FamilyImage caption, Denise had told hospice staff she wanted to experience the "horsey smell" againJoanne described the response to her appeal as "overwhelming".The visit took place on Friday 14 August, the last day that her mother was fully conscious, she said, adding: "It was the last wonderful day that we got to spend with her doing something that we know that she loved and wanted to do."Denise died the following Sunday.Image source, FamilyImage caption, Joanne said she would look back on the day with happy memoriesKerry Saunders said Denise's face "just lit up"."She was able to stroke them and feel their breath, which is exactly what she wanted," she said.The former nurse added: "I just felt so privileged to be able to fulfil one of her last wishes, and the ponies were absolutely amazing."They put their heads on her bed."She said the ponies also visited another patient after staff were asked if they could stop by a second room.Joanne said it was a "fantastic" day that she would look back on with happy memories.She said: "There's that spark of joy in otherwise what was such an emotionally difficult weekend."Follow BBC Sussex on Facebook, external, X, external, and Instagram, external and listen to BBC Radio Sussex on Sounds. Send your story ideas to southeasttoday@bbc.co.uk, external or WhatsApp us on 08081 002250.

schema.headline: Sussex horse lover's final wish fulfilled with hospice pony visit

title: Bahrain GP in Malaysia: Verstappen wins after long delays
description: Image gallerySkip image galleryImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Race day started well enough, with Malaysians treated to their first race sinc
body: Image gallerySkip image galleryImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Race day started well enough, with Malaysians treated to their first race since 2017 thanks to Bahrain paying to hold it at Sepang following unrest in the Middle EastSlide 1 of 5, Fans at Bahrain GP in Malaysia, Race day started well enough, with Malaysians treated to their first race since 2017 thanks to Bahrain paying to hold it at Sepang following unrest in the Middle EastOnce the race got under way, with the cars in their original order, Verstappen and Hamilton on the front row immediately lost ground and the Mercedes of Antonelli and Russell swept past them into first and second places.Verstappen and the Mercedes drivers took the start on intermediate tyres on the still-wet track after a torrential tropical downpour had delayed the start.Hamilton chose soft-compound slicks and immediately regretted the decision as it became apparent that the track was still far too wet for that option. He and others who chose slicks immediately dropped to the back of the field, and lost nearly a minute to the leaders in the early laps.Meanwhile, Verstappen repassed Russell for second place on lap six, and was on Antonelli's tail when a safety car was deployed to allow marshals to recover the Cadillac of Valtteri Bottas, who had spun off at Turn 13 on lap nine.The leaders took the opportunity of the safety car to pit for slick tyres, and when the race resumed four laps later, Verstappen immediately passed Antonelli at Turn Four, the Italian also losing out to Russell on the exit of the corner.From that moment on, Verstappen was total in control and he edged away into a race of his own.Behind him, Antonelli had pace on Russell and passed him on lap 21 at Turn Four, the move seemingly settling the top three positions.A late safety car caused by Alex Albon's stricken Williams led to everyone switching to fresh tyres for a four-lap dash to the flag, but again Verstappen was supreme and remained unchallenged.Even then, there was drama, as Russell pulled off just before Turn One with five laps to go before the safety car had even ended.In the immediate aftermath, Lando Norris was apparently distracted by Russell's car and had to take to the gravel at Turn One to avoid running into the back of team-mate Oscar Piastri, dropping from eighth to 11th.He recovered to ninth by the end, immediately behind Fernando Alonso, who scored points for Aston Martin for only the third time this year after their strongest performance of the year.Hamilton and the others who chose to use dry tyres at the start immediately lived to regret their decision, as they were passed by all the cars on intermediates.Within a few laps, Hamilton was nearly a minute behind the leaders and down in 17th place, his race apparently over.But he stayed out during the safety car, sticking with the soft tyres he had chosen for the start, and when the race restarted he began to pick off the cars in front of him, driving an excellent race to get back into contention for serious points.Hamilton passed car after car until by lap 24 he was on the tail of Isack Hadjar's fourth-placed Red Bull.They pitted together on lap 31, Hadjar sticking to soft tyres, and Hamilton having no choice but to move to mediums.Hamilton trailed the Frenchman for lap after lap, right on his tail, but was never quite able to get close enough to pass, despite a number of attempts, before the late safety car.That gave Hamilton the chance to switch to the preferred soft tyres, and a lap after the restart he passed Hadjar into Turn One to take the final podium position.Ferrari's Charles Leclerc also passed Hadjar in the closing laps, with Oscar Piastri taking sixth after a dispiriting weekend for McLaren, ahead of Racing Bulls' Liam Lawson and Alonso.Norris and the second Racing Bulls of Arvid Lindblad completed the top 10.After the tropical downpour, the race was initially started with formation laps behind the safety car. But immediately the problems started.Verstappen and Hamilton were the first of a number of cars that were afflicted by a software issue that left them unable to do more than crawl along.Governing body the FIA said this was caused by a combination of the weather, low speed, the mandated wet-weather energy management settings and the circuit layout. A software update removing the constraint on energy limits was issued by governing body the FIA during the subsequeby start delay to enable teams to resolve the issue. Most teams who were afflicted managed eventually to get their cars going, but the field order was jumbled, and that led to a debate as to the positions in which the cars should take the restart.The rules did not cover the situation, which was unprecedented. And although they outline positional penalties for any driver who is not able to regain his position by a certain place on the track having lost it on a formation lap, this was ignored in restarting the race in its original order.

schema.headline: Bahrain GP in Malaysia: Verstappen wins after long delays

title: Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia: Harry Benjamin's driver ratings
description: Max Verstappen - 9.5/10Hard to find much wrong this weekend. Dominant through every part of qualifying for his first pole of the season. A poor start
body: Max Verstappen - 9.5/10Hard to find much wrong this weekend. Dominant through every part of qualifying for his first pole of the season. A poor start but then recovered after losing out to both Mercedes drivers to control a hugely difficult race.Kimi Antonelli - 9/10Proving Baku was just a blip for the championship leader. Produced an excellent start to take the lead and ultimately brought home second on a weekend where Mercedes never looked entirely comfortable.Lewis Hamilton - 9.5/10A superb recovery after Ferrari's decision to start on slick tyres sent him tumbling from the front row to 18th. Hamilton fought all the way back to the podium and passed Isack Hadjar after the final safety car to complete one of his best drives of the season.Charles Leclerc - 8.5/10Close to team-mate Hamilton in qualifying before suffering the same early tyre nightmare in the race. Recovered impressively through the field to fourth and ensured Ferrari salvaged a huge result from a strategy that initially looked disastrous.Isack Hadjar - 8.5/10Third fastest in qualifying was an excellent performance before his engine penalty dropped him to eighth on the grid. A great battle with Hamilton even if he did lose out with Leclerc denying him fourth at the end too.Oscar Piastri - 7.5/10Never quite had McLaren at the sharp end but made the right early call to abandon the slicks and start from the pit lane on intermediate tyres. Recovered to sixth and comfortably beat Norris on a day when simply keeping everything clean counted for plenty.Liam Lawson- 8.5/10One of his strongest races of the year. Just missed Q3 and then made a sensational start in the wet conditions, gaining seven positions and briefly running fourth before eventually bringing his Racing Bulls home in seventh.Fernando Alonso - 8/10Aston Martin finally showed some signs of life and Alonso made sure to capitalise. Reached Q2 on merit and converted 12th on the grid into an excellent eighth-place finish. Comfortably the team's best result for some time.Lando Norris - 5.5/10A frustrating weekend that ended with an avoidable mistake. Qualified ahead of Piastri and was right behind his team-mate before the final restart, only to lose control behind the safety car and ran through the gravel, dropping him to ninth.Arvid Lindblad - 8.5/10A really impressive recovery considering he started at the very back because of his power unit penalty. Helped Lawson with a tow on Saturday and then charged through to score the final point on Sunday.Nico Hulkenberg - 7/10Missing Q2 was disappointing but he responded with a strong recovery on Sunday. Climbed from 15th on the grid to finish just outside the points and comfortably ahead of Audi team-mate Bortoleto after the Brazilian's penalty.Lance Stroll - 6.5/10A much more competitive weekend for Aston Martin generally. Stroll joined Alonso in Q2 and kept himself out of trouble through a chaotic race to finish 12th, even if his team-mate ultimately extracted more from the opportunity.Franco Colapinto - 7/10Started 21st due to grid penalties, so 13th represented a very respectable recovery. Kept things clean after his costly mistake last time out and made up plenty of ground in difficult conditions.Oliver Bearman - 5/10Another fairly anonymous weekend for Haas. Knocked out in Q1 and although he gained a couple of places during the race, 14th was about all there was to show for it.Esteban Ocon - 5/10Frustrated with Haas' qualifying run plan after going out in Q1 and never really recovered from there. Great start and was fighting well inside the top 10. Ultimately finished behind Bearman and was unable to make the changing conditions work sufficiently to threaten the points.Pierre Gasly - 5.5/10Qualifying ninth was an excellent start but Sunday unravelled almost immediately. Nearly lost the car on slicks during the formation procedure and ultimately fell all the way to 16th as Alpine's gamble failed to pay off.Carlos Sainz - 6/10Williams struggled for pace throughout the weekend but 13th represented a good qualifying. His race was then further compromised by contact with Bortoleto, for which the Audi driver was penalised, so 17th doesn't tell the whole story.Gabriel Bortoleto - 4.5/10There was plenty to like about reaching Q3 in the Audi, but the race undid that good work. Contact with Sainz earned him a penalty and left him 18th after starting inside the top 10.Sergio Perez - 4/10Qualified last and never looked likely to make meaningful progress even amid all the chaos. Reaching the chequered flag was at least something for Cadillac, but 19th completed another difficult weekend.George Russell - 8/10A far better race than his eighth place in qualifying suggested. Made an excellent start, ran inside the top three for virtually the entire afternoon and, even if he couldn't match Mercedes team-mate Antonelli, was heading for another podium before a power-unit failure stopped him with five laps remaining.Alex Albon - 4.5/10Williams lacked pace from the outset and qualifying 20th left him with an enormous amount of work to do. His eventual retirement was caused by a gearbox problem rather than a driving error, but there had been little sign of any kind of meaningful challenge before then.Valtteri Bottas - 3.5/10A weekend to forget. Qualified ahead of Cadillac team-mate Perez but admitted his decision to run slicks was a risk before spinning into the gravel on lap nine and triggering the first safety car.

title: Daughter of murdered MP Sir David Amess says politicians still at risk
description: The review is being led by former Conservative justice secretary Sir Robert Buckland, with the aim of reporting within six months.The safety of politi
body: The review is being led by former Conservative justice secretary Sir Robert Buckland, with the aim of reporting within six months.The safety of politicians has been a prominent issue in recent years since the death of former Conservative MP Ann Widdecombe in July this year, Sir David's murder in 2021 and Labour MP Jo Cox's murder in 2016.The five years since her father was killed have been "absolutely devastating and heartbreaking", his daughter told Kuenssberg, adding: "It's a very, very real situation that we're living with."She has previously called for a public inquiry into the safety of politicians so people can have "the full facts to hand, full openness, honesty, and transparency".The nearing anniversary of Sir David's murder comes after the man accused of murdering Widdecombe was also charged with preparing acts of terror, including against Reform UK leader Nigel Farage.Amess, who knew Widdecombe as a family friend and called her Aunt Ann, said: "It's absolutely so tragic and heartbreaking that now she isn't here either." She added: "My dad was murdered five years ago so if so much has changed why are we still seeing other members of parliament or former members of parliament being targeted like this."Widdecombe was not a sitting member of parliament when she died, but was a member of the Conservative Party and the member for Maidstone and the Weald from 1987 to 2010. She became a member of Reform UK in 2019.Separately, Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch confirmed to the BBC the man who pleaded guilty to sending her threatening messages also sent them to her family.Kieran Kyle, 43, pleaded guilty to two counts of sending communication of an indecent or offensive nature to Badenoch and her family when he appeared in court in September. He will be sentenced on October 29."I just think that whether it's Nigel Farage, or even Keir Starmer who had his home fire bombed, that there is a threat to politicians that is increasing and we just need to crack down on this,"  she told Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg.Asked how Badenoch coped with threats to her safety, she replied: "it's really tough, but you just have to get on with it".Reform UK's deputy leader Richard Tice, who told the BBC he also experienced threats to his safety, told the programme "this was far from where any of us want to be"."We have to find the middle ground where we're accessible but we're protected and in the overall scheme of things if that requires a bit of extra taxpayers' money, I think hopefully voters would say 'yes'."Amess said her father "loved meeting people", saying "he was one of the easier members of parliament to take a meeting with because that's what he lived for - to meet people, shake their hands, smile, help them with their problems. My dad wouldn't have wanted constituency surgeries to stop."She added that he would have wanted to be alerted to someone being reported as a potential threat.His killer, Ali Harbi Ali had been referred to the government's counter-terror programme Prevent in October 2014 but his case was closed in 2016.A review published in February 2025 found Ali's Prevent case was closed too early after "problematic" assessments.

schema.headline: Daughter of murdered MP Sir David Amess says politicians still at risk

title: Green Party members back 'Zionism is racism' conference motion
description: Green Party members have adopted a motion declaring Zionism a form of racism, in a move that has divided senior figures at the top of the party.The pa
body: Green Party members have adopted a motion declaring Zionism a form of racism, in a move that has divided senior figures at the top of the party.The party's joint deputy leaders have been at odds over the subject, with Mothin Ali backing the move, and Rachel Millward describing the wording as "problematic".Activists endorsed the policy motion, which was put forward by a group of members at the party's conference in Brighton, by 1022 votes to 813.They also voted to commit the party to supporting a "single democratic Palestinian State", after they rejected an amendment that had been backed by party leader Zack Polanski. The motion adopted by Green members defines Zionism as an ideology in support of "an ethnonationalist Jewish state" and backs a "single democratic Palestinian state in all of historic Palestine"."The real, material, manifestation of Zionism has been the historic and ongoing dehumanisation, displacement, dispossession, disenfranchisement and destruction of Palestinians," it says. It has attracted criticism from some Jewish groups, including the Board of Deputies and the Jewish Leadership Council.In a letter to the party sent ahead of the vote, the organisations said Zionism was an anti-racist movement, adding that "modern Zionism was formed in part as a response to antisemitism, creating a refuge for Jews in their ancient homeland after millennia of persecution outside it."It also raised concerns about the safety of Jewish members in the Green Party, as well as the implications for Jewish institutions in areas represented by the Greens.Debate about the motion, as well as the conflict in Gaza, has featured heavily during the conference, which is taking place after a surge in its membership following Polanski's election as leader last year. On Friday, Polanski said he believed Zionism, as it was defined in the motion, was racism.However, he said he wanted to see the reference to a single Palestinian state changed, arguing: "I don't believe we as a Green Party of England and Wales, or even the British government, should be deciding what the future settlement looks like."He had also said he wanted to see the motion amended to specify that it should not be used to discipline Jewish members attending synagogues that consider themselves Zionist.However, both amendments favoured by Polanski were rejected by Green members.A Green spokeswoman insisted the party would protect Jewish members - and they would not be persecuted for attending synagogues which defined themselves as Zionist.Speaking after the motion had been approved, chair of Jewish Greens Vivien Lichtenstein told the BBC she could consider her future in the party. Polanski himself did not vote in the debate, having left the conference early to campaign in Holborn and St Pancras, where he is standing to be the MP. A full list of candidates can be found here. He has not specified whether he supports the motion passed by members, but added his name to a joint statement from the party's five MPs and deputy leaders.The statement pledged to ensure the Green Party was "an anti-racist party in every way" and added that there was "no conflict between supporting the rights of Palestinians and the rights of Jewish people".Over the course of the three-day conference, the key figures in the party have expressed differing positions about the Zionism motion. Three of the party's five MPs - Ellie Chowns, Adrian Ramsay and Carla Denyer - had publicly opposed it, with Denyer arguing it could risk "alienating a significant proportion of Jewish people".Chowns, as well as former Greens leader Caroline Lucas both spoke against the motion during the debate.On Friday, Lucas told the BBC: "I think there is no single definition of Zionism and, irrespective of the intentions of those who put that motion, I think there is a real risk that it will be divisive and could be seen as a sign that Jewish people aren't welcome in the party."Deputy leader Mothin Ali, who had expressed support for the motion before the vote, said it was calling for "a state that's democratic, that guarantees the rights of every single person living on that land".He added that he was "absolutely not" calling all Jewish people who define themselves as Zionists racist.Following the vote, Israel's Foreign Ministry said the motion went beyond "the boundaries of legitimate political debate" and was "a stain on the history of the United Kingdom". Under Green Party rules, motions supported by members become official party policy, but will not necessarily be included in the party's manifesto at the next general election.

schema.headline: Green Party members back 'Zionism is racism' conference motion

title: England star Jude Bellingham shows he could become "one of the greatest" as he unlocks new level
description: Just a year ago, Jude Bellingham's place in the England squad was up in the air. Now he is being talked about as having the potential to be one of foo
body: Just a year ago, Jude Bellingham's place in the England squad was up in the air. Now he is being talked about as having the potential to be one of football's "greatest of all time".The Real Madrid man was left out of Thomas Tuchel's Three Lions squad in October 2025 and his place at the World Cup was called into question, with the German head coach saying Bellingham wouldn't get star treatment.But Bellingham did of course make the squad for the World Cup and was arguably his team's standout performer, finishing as England's top scorer with seven goals as they reached the semi-finals and finished third.He has already shown that he is world class with starring performances for club and country, but the way he helped England to dismantle Croatia 7-0 in the Nations League on Saturday looked like someone perhaps reaching a new level.The 23-year-old was instrumental in Rijeka, scoring as well as registering a hat-trick of assists. He even ended the match wearing the captain's armband as England inflicted the heaviest defeat in Croatia's history."Bellingham can go on to be one of the greatest players of all time," former Manchester United and Republic of Ireland midfielder Roy Keane said on ITV after the game."At this moment in time, he is an amazing footballer. The package – his running power, his delivery, his goal threat. The way he is progressing as a player, I still think there is a lot more to come from him."Bellingham, recently voted England's player of the year for the second year in a row, is now "nailed on as the 10" for the future, former England defender Matt Upson told BBC Radio 5 Live.Keane added: "He has been fantastic in possession, but what he does out of possession lifts all these other players."If you have a player that good in your team, who is amazing in possession and he's playing for Real Madrid and doing brilliant things, but his work rate off the ball... that will just inspire other players. He is a huge leader for them."England's front four will share praise for the way in which they demolished the Croatian backline.Record goalscorer Harry Kane scored twice, as did Bukayo Saka, with Anthony Gordon scoring and assisting too.And Kane will be back in the spotlight on Tuesday when he can equal Peter Shilton's all-time England men's appearance record against the Czech Republic at Wembley.In moving to 89 goals for his country, the 33-year-old again showed how irreplaceable he is for England, but, when he was rested with 20 minutes to go, it was Bellingham who took the captain's armband.And that highlighted the younger man's importance as a leader within the squad.Bellingham was also directly involved in more than two goals in an England game for the first time, and he became the first player to record three assists in a game for the Three Lions since Trent Alexander-Arnold against San Marino in November 2021.It was Bellingham's performance in front of goal that impressed former England striker Ian Wright."When Bellingham is on the pitch, he is always driving forward and going again and again," Wright said."He was involved in everything. His athleticism, his technical ability, his intensity. He never lets up, the way he gets in the box, he is always in there unmarked. He is always in there."Bellingham showed every aspect of his game against Croatia and Tuchel was asked by BBC Sport if he had gone to another level."Yes, at the moment it seems like it, and you always need to," Tuchel said."It's like you can never stand still. You have to develop and you have to push for the next level, otherwise other teams will catch up."Tuchel, who said the performance was a way to "move on" after the disappointment of England's World Cup semi-final loss to Argentina, said that he "adjusted some things" following the tournament, giving players, including Bellingham, "a lot of responsibility".Saka was part of the front four and Bellingham assisted his first goal with a high quality cross."He was amazing tonight," Saka said of Bellingham."He deserved player of the year and he deserved man of the match tonight too. He was special. "[I'm] happy to play with him and happy to have him in the England team."

schema.headline: England star Jude Bellingham shows he could become "one of the greatest" as he unlocks new level

title: Kyiv bridge hit in further Russian drone attack as German chancellor makes surprise visit
description: Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said two people were injured in the latest Russian attack. He earlier said that the Pivnichnyi Bridge's roadway was hit. K
body: Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said two people were injured in the latest Russian attack. He earlier said that the Pivnichnyi Bridge's roadway was hit. Kyiv's eight bridges across the wide Dnipro River link the western (right) and eastern (left) parts, and many of the capital's estimated three million residents rely heavily on the metro lines and trains to travel across the city.Some 500,000 vehicles use the bridges every day.The two struck bridges are still standing - but the damage and restrictions to traffic and public transport have caused gridlock in parts of the capital at times."To get from the left bank to the right one and back - it's just hell," Kyiv resident Roman told the BBC on Sunday.Large numbers of commuters cross the river, especially on weekdays. Repair teams are working to fix the damage and officials say they are planning temporary pontoon bridges, ferry services and even a tunnel under the river to keep Kyiv connected.Klitschko also said a separate Russian drone strike had damaged a heating main, adding that there would be a temporary lack of hot water in the north-eastern Desnyanskyi district as a result.Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenksy said on Sunday morning Russian drones had also attacked a warehouse in the north-eastern region of Sumy, killing one person. Meanwhile, in the central city of Dnipro, six people were injured after a communications facility was struck, he said.Ukraine's Air Force said that overnight Russia had launched 135 drones, including 52 jet-powered ones. It said that 125 projectiles had been shot down.Since Merz became chancellor in May 2025, Germany has become the single largest donor to Ukraine. He said the country "needs all our support in the coming weeks", adding: "If Russia is not stopped, its war machine will sooner or later turn against us."Zelensky said there would be "important agreements" made between Ukraine and Germany.The Ukrainian president has made repeated appeals for Western allies to provide more military support to the country, including supplying advanced interceptors that can shoot down new jet-powered Russian drones and also ballistic missiles.The Russian defence ministry said on Sunday it would intensify its strikes across Ukraine in response to comments made by Zelensky earlier this week, in which he said Kyiv would ramp up its attacks on Russian oil refineries.Russian President Vladimir Putin had earlier said his military was carrying out retaliatory attacks following Ukraine's strikes on Moscow's energy facilities, despite the fact that it was the Kremlin that had first launched such attacks.Putin began a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, and Moscow currently controls about 20% of Ukrainian territory.The Russian foreign ministry on Saturday repeated a warning for foreign citizens, including diplomats, to leave Kyiv.Responding to the warning, EU ambassador Katarína Mathernová wrote on X on Sunday: "The EU Delegation is staying. Threatening us will not stop Europe's support for Ukraine. It only reminds us why that support matters!"German ambassador to Ukraine, Boris Ruge, reacted to Mathernova's post with: "Amen - we're staying".

schema.headline: Kyiv bridge hit in further Russian drone attack as German chancellor makes surprise visit
